## **1. Introduction**

## 1.1. **Walney Extension Offshore Wind Farm**

1.1.1 Walney Extension Offshore Wind Farm (the Project) is an extension to the operational Walney I and Walney II Offshore Wind Farms (the Existing Wind Farms) in the east Irish Sea, leased as part of The Crown Estate Round 2.5 offshore wind farm development programme. The proposed development is located to the north west of the operational wind farms, approximately 19 km west south west of the Isle of Walney coast in Cumbria and 31 km south east of the Isle of Man. The site covers an area of approximately 149 km[2] . Figure 1 shows the proposed development site and potential cable route options, in relation to the Existing Wind Farms and other offshore wind farms in the area.

1.1.2 The expected maximum installed capacity of the project is 750 MW, with turbines of between 3.6 and 8.0 MW generating capacity under consideration. The total number of turbines at the site may vary between a potential maximum number of 207, 3.6 MW turbines; and a minimum number of 75, 8 MW turbines. The exact turbine choice and array layout shall be determined post‐consent. To facilitate meaningful impact assessments, and in line with the Rochdale Envelope approach, two indicative turbine layout options are presented within Chapter 4 of the Walney Extension Offshore Wind Farm Environmental Statement (ES).

**Figure 1: Location of the Project in relation to the coast of England and other wind farms in the area. Potential export cable route corridor is indicated. (Source: DONG, 2012)**

## 1.2. **Technical Report Objectives**

1.2.1 This report forms part of the assessment of the potential impacts of the Project on marine mammals. The purpose of this report is to:

- Determine the spatial extent of the study area within which the potential impacts upon marine mammals associated with the construction, operation and decommissioning phases of the Project can be assessed;

- Collate existing baseline data in relation to marine mammals for the site and surrounding areas;

- Present and analyse site‐specific survey data collected for the Project;

- Establish the importance of the proposed Project area for marine mammals, including breeding,  feeding or transiting areas (migration and commuting);

- Identify potential sensitive marine mammal receptors in relation to the Project, with consideration of both baseline data sources and site‐specific survey data; and

- Consider the importance of the Project site for sea turtles and identify any potential sensitive receptors.

1.2.2 This report considers marine mammals (cetaceans and pinnipeds), and includes sea turtles – which although not mammalian, are members of the marine megafauna. This report will provide a basis for the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) of potential impacts arising from the Project.

## **2. Policy, Guidance and Legislation**

The following legislation, policy and guidance documents, pertaining to marine mammals and offshore wind farm developments have been considered in this report.

## 2.1. **Renewable Energy Policy**

2.1.1 The overarching National Policy Statement (NPS) for Energy (EN‐1) (DECC, 2011) forms part of a suite of NPSs issued by the Secretary of State for Energy and Climate Change. It sets out Government policy, high level objectives and regulatory framework for new Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIPs) for the delivery of major energy infrastructure. Under the Planning Act 2008, EN‐1, combined with the relevant technology‐specific energy NPS[1] , provides the primary basis for assessment and recommendations by the Planning Inspectorate (PINS) as the examining authority, and for decisions made by the Secretary of State for Energy and Climate Change.

2.1.2 NPS EN‐3, for Renewable Energy Infrastructure (DECC, 2011), taken together with EN‐1, sets out the policy and provides the basis to enable PINS to examine and make recommendations on applications for nationally significant renewable energy developments in England and Wales. In addition to setting the policy regarding the generic biodiversity impacts of offshore wind, EN‐3 makes specific reference to potential impacts on marine mammals due to noise from piling and the potential associated requirement for a European Protected Species (EPS) licence.

> 1 Overarching National Policy Statement for Energy (EN‐1), paragraph 1.4.1

2.1.3 EN‐3 also makes recommendations on the content of Environmental Impact Assessment

(EIA) for marine mammals. This should include, as appropriate:

- Likely feeding areas;

- Known birthing areas/haul out sites;

- Nursery grounds;

- Known migration or commuting routes;

- Duration of the potentially disturbing activity including cumulative/in‐combination effects with other plans or projects;

- Baseline noise levels;

- Predicted noise levels in relation to mortality, Permanent Threshold Shift (PTS) and Temporary Threshold Shift (TTS);

- Soft‐start noise levels according to proposed hammer and pile design; and

- Operational noise.

2.1.4 EN‐3 notes that the method and timing of construction, and the turbine foundation type for offshore wind farms, can be designed so as to minimise disturbance effects on marine mammals, and that this design should satisfy the regulator.

2.1.5 In terms of mitigation, EN‐3 requires that the following measures are considered in any assessment for marine mammals:

- Monitoring of the surrounding area before and during piling activities;

- 24‐hour working practices employed during construction so that the overall construction programme and the potential for impacts on marine mammal communities is reduced in time; and

- Soft start procedures for pile driving allowing marine mammals in the area disturbed by the sound levels to move away from the piling before significant adverse impacts are caused.

## 2.3. **Guidance**

2.3.1 A number of guidance documents are available in relation to the impacts of offshore wind farms on marine mammals. These have been consulted during the preparation of this report and include:

- Guidelines for Ecological Impact Assessment (EcIA) in Britain and Ireland, Marine and Coastal Institute for Ecology and Environmental Management (IEEM), (2010);

- Approaches to Marine Mammal Monitoring at Marine Renewable Energy Developments Final Report. Report by The Sea Mammal Research Unit on behalf of The Crown Estate. (2010);

- Common Standards Monitoring Guidance for Marine Mammals, Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC), (2005);

- Statutory Nature Conservation Agency Protocol for  Minimising the Risk of Injury to Marine Mammals from Piling Noise, JNCC (2010[a] ); and

- The Protection of Marine European Protected Species From Injury and Disturbance: Guidance for the marine Area in England and Wales and the UK Offshore Marine Area (draft), JNCC _et. al_ ., (2010[b] ).

On the advice of JNCC, this report makes use of the density and abundance calculations performed for the SCANS II surveys, to provide population estimates for different marine mammal species across regional areas.

## 3.2.

## **The Joint Cetacean Protocol (JCP)**

3.2.1 The Joint Cetacean Protocol (JCP) has been established by the Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC), to facilitate the reporting requirements of the Habitats Directive. The  JCP provides an updated data resource for cetaceans in the UK and comprises a set of standards for the integration of cetacean abundance and distribution data collected in European waters. The next JCP guidance document, Phase 3 “Joint Cetacean Protocol, marine renewables industry data guide” is expected to be released in early 2013 and is therefore unavailable at the time of writing.

3.2.2 The latest advice from JNCC is that initial outputs from previous phases of JCP should no longer be used in planning applications, due to some issues with possibly over‐inflated density estimates (JNCC _Pers. Comm._ , May 2012). Instead, applicants should make use of the best available data, including the Small Cetaceans in the European Atlantic and North Sea (SCANS) data sets and the Atlas of cetacean abundance in north‐west European waters (Reid, _et. al.,_ 2003) combined with site specific surveys.

## 3.3.

## **Small Cetaceans in the European Atlantic and North Sea (SCANS)**

3.3.1 The first SCANS project survey took place in the July 1994. The survey was conducted by teams of observers on research ships and small aircraft across different survey blocks (see Appendix 1 for a figure of the SCANS II survey blocks) and used line transect methods to collect distance sampling data to estimate the number of animals within each survey block area. The SCANS project had key three aims;

1. to determine absolute abundance of cetacean populations across the survey area;

2. to develop and test methods to monitor cetaceans and to develop a framework for management of bycatch (the first SCANS survey did not cover the Irish Sea region,

however In 2005 the SCANS II project was undertaken to update the estimates provided in SCANS); and,

3. to monitor cetacean abundance between decades and to survey additional areas, including the Irish Sea, survey block O.

3.3.2 Using the survey data collected, calculations of animal density and abundance were performed for the different survey blocks and surface density maps were produced for the areas surveyed. Total estimates were also calculated by combining abundance estimates for both shipboard and aerial surveys, for each of the SCANS II survey blocks (Sea Mammal Research Unit (SMRU), 2006). On the advice of JNCC, this report makes use of the density and abundance calculations performed for the SCANS II surveys, to provide population estimates for different marine mammal species across regional areas.

## **4. Study Area**

4.1. **Introduction**

4.1.1 Marine mammals are highly mobile species, resulting in a wide distribution across preferred habitats in UK waters. This report considers the distribution and abundance of marine mammals known to occur within or adjacent to the Project area (see Section 4.1), within the wider, regional context of the Irish Sea (The regional area; see Section 4.2). This allows shorter term, site specific information, collected through surveys, to be considered alongside longer term, regional information.

## 4.2. **The Project area**

4.2.1 The Project area includes the proposed wind farm development, ( turbines, inter‐array cabling and offshore substations) and a 4 km buffer (zone of influence) area.

## 4.3. **The regional area**

4.3.1 The regional area considered is the Irish Sea, which encompasses the waters off the coasts of Wales, north‐west England and east coasts of Ireland and Northern Ireland. Within the SCANS II project, this area is defined as the Irish Sea survey block O (Hammond _et. al_ ., 2006) and covers an area of 45,417 km[2] . This assessment is based on this indicative regional area for the Irish Sea (see Figure 2). However, due to the wide ranging migratory nature of marine mammals, reference to wider populations including the west coast survey area and the total SCANS II study region (the European Atlantic Continental Shelf) is also made).

**Figure 2: Project area and indicative regional area of the Irish Sea**

## **5. Baseline Environment:  Marine mammals**

## 5.1. **Introduction**

5.1.1 More than 20 species of cetacean have been recorded in UK waters, 18 of which have been recorded in the Irish Sea region. However, only five of these species are known to occur regularly within the Irish Sea and these include;

- Harbour Porpoise ( _Phocoena phocoena_ );

- Bottlenose Dolphin ( _Tursiops truncatus_ );

- Short‐beaked Common Dolphin _(Delphinus delphis)_ ;

- Risso’s Dolphin _(Grampus griseus)_ ; and,

- Minke Whale ( _Balaenoptera acutorostrata_ ) .

5.1.2 The remaining species, including white‐beaked dolphin _(Lagenorhynchus albirostris)_ , are considered to be rare or occasional visitors  (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2005; Baines and Evans, 2009).

5.1.3 Only two pinniped species are known to live and breed in UK waters:

- Grey Seal _(Halichoerus grypus)_ ; and,

- Harbour or Common Seal _(Phoca vitulina)._

5.1.4 Within the UK harbour seals generally have a much wider distribution than grey seal: however, very few are known to occur in the Irish Sea region, the greatest concentrations of these species occurring in Scottish waters, Northern Ireland and Norfolk at Blakeney Point (SCOS, 2011). Within the Irish Sea region, the majority of haul out sites for grey seal are located on the coast of Wales and Ireland. However, the Isle of Man also supports some important sites including the Calf of Man, The Sound, Langness and Maughold. The Calf of Man is also a pupping site for small numbers of grey seals (Hanley _et. al.,_ 2012).

5.1.5 To inform assessment of the potential importance of the Project site for key marine mammal species, a combination of boat‐based and aerial surveys were surveys were carried out concurrently with ornithological surveys.  Boat‐based surveys were undertaken from June 2011 to September 2011, and from February to November 2012 by the Centre for Marine and Coastal Studies Ltd (CMACS).  Aerial digital imagery surveys were undertaken between November 2010 and October 2012 by the Danish Centre for Environment and Energy (DCE, formerly NERI). Further information on survey methodologies are provided in Section 6.

5.1.6 Although not regularly recorded within the Irish Sea, white‐beaked dolphin and leatherback turtles were recorded in site specific surveys undertaken for the existing and proposed wind farms sites.

## 5.2. **Irish Sea marine mammals not recorded in Project site survey**

5.2.1 The following marine mammal species are known to occur within the in the Irish Sea, but were not recorded in Project site‐specific survey:

- Bottlenose Dolphin;

- Short‐beaked Common Dolphin;

- Risso’s Dolphin;

- Minke Whale; and

- Harbour Seal.

5.2.2 The following sections provide a brief overview of the population characteristics of each of these species.

## **Bottlenose Dolphin**

5.2.3 Bottlenose dolphins are distributed throughout tropical and temperate seas worldwide, from shallow estuaries to deep ocean waters beyond the continental shelf (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003). In UK waters, bottlenose dolphin occur off the north‐east and south‐west coast of Scotland, in the Irish Sea and the English Channel (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2005). In coastal waters bottlenose dolphins often favour river estuaries, headlands or sandbanks (Lewis and Evans, 1993).

5.2.4 Bottlenose dolphin are large animals, growing to a length of 4 m in North Atlantic waters. They are social, forming groups of between two and twenty‐five individuals, with larger groups occurring in deeper waters. They feed on a wide variety of prey, including, benthic and pelagic fish (haddock, cod, hake, mullet, sprat and sandeels) along with cephalopods and shellfish (Reid _et. al_ ., 2003).

5.2.5 In the Irish Sea the bottlenose dolphin is recorded frequently, second only to the harbour porpoise, and has a predominantly coastal distribution (although low densities have been recorded offshore, particularly in St George’s Channel and the south‐west of the Irish Sea (Baines and Evans, 2009)). Concentrations of bottlenose dolphin in the Irish Sea occur around Cardigan Bay in Wales and the south‐east coast of Ireland (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2005). In Welsh and Irish Seas seasonal differences in group size and dispersion are noted.  In summer, dolphins tend to occur mainly in small groups near the coast.  In winter, they disperse more widely and generally northwards, where they may form very large groups. Bottlenose dolphins breed throughout their range, with calves observed in most months of the year (Baines and Evans, 2009).

5.2.6 Figure 3 shows annual bottlenose dolphin sightings rates taken from the Cetacean Atlas (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003). This confirms a predominantly coastal distribution with concentrations around north‐east Scotland, south‐west Ireland and the southern Irish Sea off the coast of Wales. The SCANS II estimate of bottlenose dolphin abundance in the Irish Sea survey block is relatively low at 235 animals, while the estimate for the total SCANS II study area (European Atlantic waters, Appendix 1) is 16,485. The 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the total survey area estimate is 7,463 – 36,421 (Hammond _et. al.,_ in review). Confidence Intervals for individual survey blocks are not available within the SCANS II report, at the time of writing. Considering the general distribution of bottlenose dolphin across UK waters the SCANS II estimates for the western coast of the UK (Survey Blocks N, O, P , Q and R) is considered appropriate. ## **Short‐beaked Common Dolphin**

5.2.8 Short‐beaked common dolphin (common dolphin) are generally associated with warmer waters (10 – 20 °C) and the species is widely, although not continuously, distributed throughout the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, in warmer temperate and tropical waters (Culik, 2010[a] ). Common dolphin generally occur offshore but have been observed closer to shore, within the continental shelf.

5.2.9 The common dolphin is a small sociable dolphin. Females grow to a length of approximately 2.1 m and males approximately 2.4 m. Average group size  for the common dolphin is between six and ten individuals, although larger groups of dozens or even hundreds have been recorded (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003). The main prey types are small, pelagic schooling fish such as, mackerel, sprat, anchovy and squid (Culik, 2010[a] ).

5.2.10 Figure 4 presents the distribution of common dolphin sightings rates from the Cetacean Atlas (Reid, _et. al.,_ 2003). In Irish waters, the common dolphin regularly occurs in the Western Isles, south and west of Ireland, the English Channel and the Celtic Sea. It is mainly a summer visitor within the Irish Sea and is regularly observed in the far south of the region during summer months, although it may remain in Celtic waters into November (Hammond _et. al_ ., 2005; Baines and Evans, 2009). The species has a largely offshore distribution centred upon the Celtic Deep at the southern end of the Irish Sea, where water depths range from 50 ‐ 150 m.

5.2.11 The SCANS II estimate of common dolphin abundance for the Irish Sea survey block is relatively low, at 826 individuals.  However, the estimate for the total SCANS II study area is 52,063. The 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the total survey area estimate is 32,239 – 84,335 (Hammond _et. al.,_ in review). Considering the general distribution of common dolphin in UK waters the reference population for this species incorporates SCANS II estimates for the western coast of the UK (survey blocks N, O, P, Q and R). A map depicting the SCANS II survey area and Survey Blocks is provided in Appendix 1.

## **Risso’s Dolphin**

5.2.13 Risso’s dolphin are widely distributed throughout tropical and temperate waters. A major concentration occurs in the Western Isles and they are also observed in the Northern Isles, Irish Sea and off the south‐west coast of Ireland (Figure 5). Risso’s dolphin mainly occur offshore, beyond the continental shelf, where they are thought to feed on vertically migrant and mesopelagic cephalopods and small fish (Kruse _et. al.,_ 1999) and prefer depths of 200 – 1000 m along steeper sections of the upper continental slope.

5.2.14 Risso’s dolphin is a large dolphin growing to around 3.5 m in length. The average group size is around 30 individuals, with groups generally ranging between one and 100 individuals. They have been recorded singly and in large aggregations of up to several hundred or even thousands of animals (Kruse _et. al_ ., 1999). They are also known to regularly associate with other species of cetaceans (Culik, 2010[b] ).

5.2.15 Within the Irish Sea, Risso’s dolphins have a relatively localised distribution around the coast of Wales, including west Pembrokeshire, the western end of the Lleyn Peninsula and

Anglesey, the south‐east coast of Ireland, and waters around the northern Isle of Man. The species is mainly a summer and autumn visitor, with the highest sightings rates in the period July to September (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2005; Baines and Evans, 2009).

5.2.16 There are very few population estimates for Risso’s dolphin in recent literature and no population assessment exists for Risso’s dolphins in north‐east Atlantic waters (Simmonds and Wharam, 2008). The SCANS II survey was not able to provide robust estimates for Risso’s dolphins as there were too few observations during surveys. Therefore, at the time of this assessment, the present status and abundance of Risso’s dolphins occurring in UK waters is not known. However, the forthcoming JCP datasets and guidance will include advice on assessment of Risso’s dolphin.

## **Minke Whale**

5.2.17 Minke whale are widely distributed throughout the northern hemisphere in tropical, temperate and polar waters and occur throughout waters around the UK (Reid _et. al_ ., 2003). However, the species appears to be more abundant in the northern and western North Sea, on the continental shelf  in water depths of 200 m or more (Hammond _et. al_ ., 2005). Within

Irish and Welsh waters minke whales have a largely offshore distribution and are more localised (Baines and Evans, 2009). Although the species occurs year round on the north‐west European continental shelf most sightings have been made during spring and September (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003).

5.2.18 They grow to a length of 7 – 8.5 m and feed on a wide variety of prey species compared to other baleen whales, including, herring, cod, haddock and sandeel, as well as krill and pteropods (Haug _et. al_ ., 1995; Nordoy _et. al_ ., 1995). Minke whales are usually seen as individuals or in pairs although they can form groups when feeding of between ten and fifteen individuals. When feeding they demonstrate some site fidelity, as observed through photo‐ identification studies conducted by Dorsey _et. al_ . (1990).

5.2.19 Figure 6 shows the annual minke whale sightings rate and distribution around the UK from the Cetacean Atlas (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003). Sightings of minke whale are more frequent in northern UK waters and are concentrated around the north‐west and south‐east coasts of Scotland, and the north‐east coast of England. Smaller concentrations also occur around the south coast of Ireland.

5.2.20 Figure 7 shows the SCANS II surface density map for minke whale, including the Irish Sea. General patterns are comparable to the Cetacean Atlas (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003), in that higher densities are seen off the coast of Scotland, and north‐east England, although greater densities are apparent further offshore, in line with observations made by Baines and Evans (2009). Densities for the Irish Sea are low; between 0.01 and 0.05 animals per km[2] . The SCANS II Irish Sea minke whale population is estimated at 1,070 animals, while the European Atlantic population (SCANS II survey area) is estimated at 18,958. The 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the total survey area estimate is 9,798 – 36,680 (Hammond _et. al.,_ in review).

5.2.21 Given the general offshore density and distribution of minke whale in northern UK waters and off the southern coast of Ireland, the estimated UK west coast population (SCANS II survey blocks N, O, P, Q and R ) is considered an appropriate reference population. ## **Harbour Seal**

5.2.22 Harbour seals have a widespread circumpolar distribution along the coasts of the North Pacific and North Atlantic, with around 30% of the European population occurring in the UK. Approximately 4% of the world’s harbour seals are found in the UK and around 80% of the UK harbour seal population is located in Scotland (Defra, 2010). There are a few local concentrations around estuaries on the east coast of England and Scotland, with a more widespread distribution along the Western Isles and the coast of Northern Ireland (Hammond _et. al_ ., 2005; SCOS, 2011).

5.2.23 Harbour seals are long‐lived and feed on a wide variety of prey species, with fish (sandeel, gadoids, herring, sprat, and flatfish) and cephalopods forming the bulk of their diet (Thompson _et. al.,_ 1998). Harbour seals normally forage within 40 to 50 km of a haul‐out site and haul‐out throughout the year, generally in sheltered waters, such as sandbanks and estuaries They come ashore to give birth, rest, and moult and are considered to be generalist predators in coastal waters. Pupping, followed by moulting occurs during the summer months, between June and August (SCOS, 2011). Populations of harbour seals are considered non‐ migratory, but the species use a wide range of habitats across their geographical distribution (Bigg, 1981).

5.2.24 The harbour seal population across parts of the UK has suffered decline in recent years. Two outbreaks of phocine distemper virus (PDV) seriously affected the harbour seal population in eastern England with 50% mortality of the total population in 1988 and 22% mortality in 2002. Harbour seals in eastern England took three years to recover from the 1988 outbreak and have yet to begin recovery following the 2002 outbreak, compared to populations elsewhere in Europe, which have shown  immediate and rapid recovery. Further, harbour seal numbers have declined significantly in Shetland, Orkney and the on east coast of Scotland by more than 50% since 2001 and the causes of these localised declines are not yet known (Defra, 2010).

5.2.25 The most recent UK harbour seal population estimate was 36,050 individuals in 2010 (SCOS, 2011). Estimates of harbour seal populations within the Irish Sea are provided in Hammond _et. al._ (2005). They are considered rare in Manx waters, and the species is not found to breed in Welsh waters (Baines and Evans, 2009; Hanley _et. al_ ., 2012). Although there are numbers along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland, few harbour seals are known to occur in the Irish Sea (SCOS, 2011). Despite the relatively small concentration of harbour seals within the Irish Sea (compared to the much more common grey seal) the Irish Sea population (SCOS, 2011) is considered an appropriate reference population for this species, given the known foraging range and distribution off the coast of Northern Ireland. 5.3. **Irish Sea Marine mammals recorded in Project surveys** 5.3.1 Three marine mammal species were recorded in site specific surveys, including: harbour porpoise, grey seal and white beaked dolphin.  However, white beaked dolphin were only

recorded in very low numbers. In addition, one leatherback turtle was also recorded. The following sections provide a detailed review of the population characteristics of each of these species, both in the UK and in Irish waters.

## **Harbour Porpoise**

5.3.2 Harbour porpoise are the smallest and most frequently observed of all the cetaceans found in the UK and European continental shelf waters. Around the UK, harbour porpoise are most abundant off the north‐west and east of Scotland, western and southern Ireland, Wales and south‐west England and are likely to be the most numerous marine mammal within the Irish Sea (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2005). There are particular concentrations in southern parts of the Irish Sea, where the species occurs year round (Hammond _et. al_ ., 2005). They are coastal in nature, frequenting shallow bays, estuaries and tidal channels less than 200 m in depth and the majority of sightings occurring within 10 km of the coast (RBA Ltd., 2005). Generally harbour porpoise are solitary animals, but may form small groups of up to three individuals.

5.3.3 The harbour porpoise is a highly mobile cetacean species, with local abundance and distribution likely to depend on prey distribution (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2005). Seasonal movements are thought to be due to changes in prey availability, with harbour porpoise remaining inshore in the summer and moving further offshore during the winter period (Santos and Pierce, 2003).  They feed on a wide variety of small fish species, such as gadoids, herring, sandeel, pout and gobies (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003). Studies of harbour porpoise foraging behaviour in the UK suggest that foraging is closely related to the tidal cycle. These studies indicate that channels created by the tidal race are used by harbour porpoise to herd and catch pelagic shoaling fish which become concentrated (RBA Ltd., 2005).

5.3.4 Harbour porpoise are likely to breed throughout areas where they are distributed (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2005). Mating occurs in the summer, with an 11 month gestation period and a calving interval usually every two years. Around the British Isles, the majority of births have been recorded between May and August (RBA Ltd., 2005). Within the Irish Sea Calves occur throughout the region (Baines and Evans, 2009).

5.3.5 Figure 9 shows the annual harbour porpoise sighting rates and distribution around the UK from the Cetacean Atlas (Reid _et. al_ ., 2003). This demonstrates that harbour porpoise are widely distributed throughout  UK waters, with concentrations along the eastern coast of England, off the western coast of Scotland and the southern Irish Sea and south‐west Ireland.

**Figure 9: Distribution of harbour porpoise in the North Atlantic (Source: Reid** _**et. al.,**_ **2003)**

5.3.6 Berrow _et al._ (2010) analysed sighting and stranding data from 2000‐2009 to determine the distribution and relative abundance of cetaceans around the Irish coast, including seasonal and geographical factors, and to identify critical habitats and potential effects. Harbour porpoise were the most widespread of all cetacean species in Ireland and were observed in all inshore waters around the entire coastline. The majority of records were within 10 km of the coast, with approximately 50% between June and September, and sightings remained high into autumn and early winter at well watched sights. The lowest abundance was recorded in spring.

5.3.7 Studies of harbour porpoise distribution in Welsh and Irish waters by Baines and Evans (2009) identified ‘hot spots’ around Anglesey and off the Pembrokeshire coast, and to a lesser extent off the south coast of the Lleyn Peninsula, in southern Cardigan Bay, and in the Bristol Channel off the south coast of Wales. Figure 10 shows interpolated long term mean sightings rates for harbour porpoise within the Irish Sea and around the Project area between 1990 and 2007.

5.3.8 Figure 11 shows the harbour porpoise surface density map for the SCANS II area, including the Irish Sea. As seen in Cetacean Atlas, SCANS II data also indicate that harbour porpoise are distributed throughout UK waters, with highest densities recorded around the east coast of England off the Norfolk coast and the Celtic Sea. Although harbour porpoise are known to be present in the Irish Sea, they occur at relatively low densities (0.2 to 0.5 animals per km[2] ).

5.3.9 Although the original SCANS project did not include the Irish Sea area, general trends in harbour porpoise distribution were assessed using data available from both the 1994 and 2005 surveys. This indicated large scale changes in harbour porpoise distribution, with concentrations shifting from north eastern UK and Denmark to the southern North Sea. It was considered that this trend was the likely due to changing availability of principle prey sources (SMRU, 2006).

5.3.10 The Wetlands and Wildlife Trust carried out a study of cetaceans and pinnipeds around the UK and this included a review of harbour porpoise distribution (WWT, 2009 – see Table 2). Aerial surveys were undertaken over the period 2001 to 2008, primarily for waterbirds and including marine mammals, turtles, sharks and sunfish. The methods used were comparable to the SCANS project (Hammond _et. al.,_ 2002). This data was used to calculate the relative densities of harbour porpoise by normalising the number of observations by coverage (per 2 km Ordnance Survey Great Britain grid cell).  The estimated densities derived for harbour porpoise are shown in  Figure 12.  WWT data show a similar distribution to that presented in the Cetacean Atlas (Reid et. al., 2003) and the SCANS II survey, with greater densities recorded off the east coast of England. Within the Irish Sea, higher concentrations are recorded towards the south with fewer records to the north and adjacent to the Isle of Man. Relative densities recorded for the Irish Sea are between 0.001 and 0.1 animals per km[2] .

## **White‐Beaked Dolphin**

5.3.13 White‐beaked dolphin occurs on the continental shelf around west and northern Scotland and in the northern North Sea.  The species tends to prefer water depths between 50 m and 100 m and rarely occur in waters as deep as 200 m (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003). They are much less common in the southern North Sea, the English Channel and are considered only occasional visitors to the Irish Sea. Although present over the continental shelf year round in UK coastal waters, the species has been observed most frequently between June and October (Northridge _et. al.,_ 1995). Figure 13 demonstrates white‐beaked dolphin distribution in UK waters from the Cetacean Atlas (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003).

5.3.14 White‐beaked dolphins are relatively small dolphins growing to around 2.5 to 2.7 m in length with a distinctive white beak. They are usually found in schools numbering less than ten individuals, although schools of 50 are not uncommon, and larger groups of 100 to 500 animals have been observed in their northern ranges and in the North Sea (Reid _et. al.,_ 2003).

5.3.15 White‐beaked dolphin prey consists of a variety of fish including: mackerel, herring, cod, whiting and hake as well various species of sandeels, flatfish, gobies and octopus, although cod, whiting and hake appear to be the predominant prey source (Kinze _et. al_ ., 1997; Reid _et. al.,_ 2003).

5.3.16 The SCANS II population estimate of white‐beaked dolphin abundance for the Irish Sea is low, 307 animals, due to their low occurrence within the region. However, the population estimate for the total SCANS II study region is 16,536 The 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the total survey area estimate is 9,245 – 29,586 (Hammond _et. al.,_ in review). When considering the general distribution of white‐beaked dolphin around the UK, with concentrations around

the north‐western Scottish coast, the western coast of the UK reference population (SCANS Survey Blocks N, O, P, Q and R) is considered appropriate for this species. A map depicting the SCANS II survey area and Survey Blocks is provided in Appendix 1.

## **Grey Seal**

5.3.18 Grey seals are long lived animals and are the larger of the two resident UK seal species. Around 111,000 grey seals breed in UK waters, approximately 38% of the global grey seal population, with a large proportion of these (around 90%) belonging to Scottish colonies (SCOS, 2011). Following the cessation of culling in the 1970’s, the grey seal population experienced decades of increasing size. The UK population now appears to be levelling with populations increasing at only a small number of colonies (Defra, 2010).

5.3.19 The preferred habitat of grey seal comprises exposed coasts, with haul‐out sites occurring on offshore rocks, remote beaches, sea cave beaches and uninhabited islands (RBA Ltd., 2005). They return to land to rest, breed and during their annual moult. The annual moult generally occurs over the winter months (December to March), while pupping usually occurs between September and November and seals will spend the majority of their time on land during this period (Hanley _et. al.,_ 2012).

5.3.20 Grey seals are common across the Irish Sea, although there are clear concentrations around the Scottish coast. Within the Irish Sea region, grey seals frequent the coasts of

Northern Ireland, Wales and the southern Irish Sea. Grey seals are also found around the coasts of the Isle of Man, and the Calf of Man is noted as a minor colony and pupping site for small numbers of grey seals (Hanley _et. al_ ., 2012).

5.3.21 In the Irish Sea region grey seals are an important predator. They feed mainly from the seabed at depths of up to 100 m, taking a wide variety of prey species including sandeel, cod, gadoids and flatfish, although this varies seasonally (RBA Ltd., 2005).  Studies in the western Irish Sea found that grey seals predominantly feed on gadoids and flatfish, depending on the geographic location of the haul‐out sites (Keily et. al., 2000). Tracking of individual seals has shown that foraging occurs within 100 km of a haul‐out site and that seals will occasionally move to a new haul‐out site and begin foraging in a new region (SCOS, 2011) (Figure 14).

Estimated usage represents the estimated number of animals using different locations at sea during the time the  population spends offshore . It should be noted that this is higher than total usage per time unit, because seals also spend time on shore.

Estimates were made using pup census data, supported by photo‐identification mark and recapture data, and provided estimates between 5,198 and 6,976 seals. **Leatherback Turtle**

5.3.25 The leatherback turtle is the largest of all turtles and the fourth largest modern reptile, growing up to 2 m long (Defra, 2010).  It is a regular visitor to UK waters, albeit in very small numbers and is more frequently reported than any other marine turtle in British waters (JNCC, 2007). Since 1954 to the present, there have been 618 leatherback turtles recorded in the UK and in the past ten years, an average of 33 leatherback turtles have been recorded each year (with a minimum of 15 and a maximum of 62). Up to 70% of these records were recorded in the Western Channel, Celtic Sea and Irish Sea (Defra, 2010). Recent studies have suggested that the waters of the UK represent the northern most limit of routine seasonal leatherback foraging migrations, although there have been records of individuals as far north as Iceland and Norway (Marabuni, 2010).

5.3.26 Leatherback turtles feed primarily on jellyfish and other gelatinous zooplankton (Hays _et. al.,_ 2004) and associations between leatherback turtles and jellyfish concentrations have been reported (Paladino _et. al.,_ 1990). It is thought that the waters surrounding the UK therefore offer good foraging habitat for this species (Houghton _et. al.,_ 2006).

5.3.27 Leatherback turtles are critically endangered globally, with Pacific populations declining at an increasing rate (Defra, 2010), although the number of leatherbacks in the Atlantic appears to be stable. Declining populations are thought to be due to egg harvest, fisheries by‐ catch and coastal development combined with highly variable food source availability (Houghton _et. al.,_ 2006). The global nesting population of leatherback turtles was estimated at around 35,000 females in 1995 and approximately 80% of these were recorded from nesting sites in the Atlantic (Spotila _et. al.,_ 1996). However, at present, the population of leatherback turtles, both in the UK and the Irish Sea, is unknown (JNCC, 2007).

5.3.28 Leatherback turtles have also been considered in previous offshore wind farm applications in the Irish Sea.  Both West of Duddon Sands and Rhyl Flats acknowledged the rare presence of turtles in the surrounding area, but deemed the occurrence too insignificant to warrant assessment, on account of their marginal use of the Irish Sea and expected lower levels of sensitivity to noise. Generally, leatherback turtles are not thought to be any more sensitive to noise than cetaceans, so impact assessment and mitigation plans for cetaceans should also be adequate for turtles (Houghton _et. al.,_ 2006).

5.3.29 Figure 17 presents the distribution of sightings of leatherback turtles around UK waters since 1998, from the ‘TURTLE’ database (Pierpoint and Penrose, 2002). These data are largely derived from opportunistic sightings and therefore cannot be used to calculate a population estimate (JNCC, 2007).  This demonstrates that leatherback turtles have been recorded around UK waters and within the Irish Sea, with the greatest concentrations of sightings off Cornwall, Wales and the Solway Firth.

5.3.30 Considering the very low presence of leatherback turtles in UK waters, combined with the large migratory range of the species and the lack of data to support a UK population estimate, the reference population for this species considers both the average annual count data in UK waters and the nesting population of breeding females in the Atlantic. However it should be noted that Leatherback turtles are not resident to the Irish Sea, but migrate to the area, most likely due to foraging habitat afforded. They are transient in UK waters and hence

the Irish Sea population of leatherback turtles will be far lower than the population of the wider Atlantic.  Table 10 presents a summary of the leatherback turtle status and distribution.

## **6. Survey and Modelling Methods**

Site‐specific marine mammal surveys have been carried out across the Project site and 4km buffer, to inform assessment of the potential importance of the Project site for key marine mammal species. To inform the assessment of noise impacts on marine mammals, noise modelling has been undertaken by Subacoustech Environmental.

## 6.1. **Boat‐based Surveys**

6.1.1 Marine mammal surveys were carried out concurrently with ornithological boat‐based surveys from June 2011 to September 2011, and from February to November 2012 by the Centre for Marine and Coastal Studies Ltd (CMACS).  The survey schedule was designed to ensure surveys were conducted to when peak sightings for ornithological and marine species were expected. Survey methodology was in line with the standards recommended by Collaborative Offshore Wind Research Into the Environment (COWRIE) in Camphuysen _et. al._ (2004). Two observers were present during each survey, with at least one being a JNCC accredited marine mammal observer. Each observer was equipped with binoculars and a dictaphone (voice recorder) to make audio records of marine mammal sightings.

6.1.2 The survey transects were spaced 4 km apart, with marine mammals recorded within 300 m either side of the transect and covered a survey area that included the wind farm footprint and 4 km buffer (Project area), (see Figure 17, Section 8.1). One additional transect was completed that fell outside the Project area (remaining survey extent).

6.1.3 The following information was recorded with each marine mammal sighting: species; number; time of observation; distance band (distance from the vessel); position relative to the vessel; direction of movement/bearing from the vessel and, if possible, behaviour and age class (CMACS, 2012).

## 6.2. **Aerial Surveys**

6.2.1 Twenty two aerial digital imagery surveys were undertaken between November 2010 and October 2012 by the Danish Centre for Environment and Energy (DCE, formerly NERI) (Petersen _et. al.,_ 2012). Surveys were conducted along 17 transects spaced 2 km apart, across the Project area, including the wind farm and 4 km buffer. Cameras were operated from a twin engine aircraft at an altitude of 475 m. on shore, the resulting images were processed via an automated system which recognises potential birds and marine mammals. These images were then identified to species level, where possible, by trained ecologists. A map demonstrating aerial survey transects is provided in Appendix 2.

## 6.3. **Noise Modelling Methodology**

6.3.1 Underwater noise modelling has been carried out to inform the assessment of potential impacts on marine mammals during Project development (Subacoustech Ltd, YEAR). Evidence and experience from other wind farm developments and studies has shown that levels of underwater noise generated are greatest during construction activities and that the noise generated by piling operations has the greatest impact on marine mammals (Subacoustech, 2012). Therefore, noise modelling provides a means of assessing:  the level of noise output at a given location, assuming a particular type of construction methodology; and the potential effect (e.g. injurious or behavioural) on specific marine mammal species (Subacoustech, 2012).

## **Noise models**

6.3.2 To undertake the assessment of subsea noise, Subacoustech have used two different in‐ house models; SPEAR (the Simple Propagation Estimator and Ranking) and INSPIRE (the Impulse Noise Sound Propagation and Impact Range Estimator).

6.3.3 The SPEAR model is based on a substantial database of noise measurements from various sources and uses a simple Source Level and Transmission Loss (SL‐TL) model for calculating impact ranges and the area of sea rendered potentially unusable for a species. The SPEAR model ranks activities that produce underwater noise in order of significance, to enable the critical activities to be identified and evaluated. Typically the model is used to identify the effect of a range of noise sources on a particular species or the effect of a particular noise source on a range of animals.

6.3.4 The INSPIRE model estimates the propagation of impulsive noise in shallow water. Transmission of sound underwater is highly variable due to local bathymetry and physical conditions. In shallow water environments, lower frequency sounds generally propagate more efficiently than high frequency sounds. Using INSPIRE, 180 equally spaced transects have been modelled for each pile location.  Transects were equally spaced at two degree intervals for 360 degrees around the pile position. Bathymetry and depth profiles were included in modelling to take into account associated changes in sound transmission.

6.3.5 Both the SPEAR and INSPIRE models produce dBht ( _Species_ ) and Sound Exposure Levels (SEL) metrics to provide both behavioural and injury based measures of the effects of noise. These metrics are explained in more detail in Section 6.1.5 below.

## **Modelling Scenarios**

6.3.6 With respect to impacts on marine mammals at the Project site, two different types of piled foundations are being considered: monopiles and jackets. Installation of the larger monopile foundations (9m) has the potential to generate a greater level of noise than installation of the smaller pin piles (3m) associated with jacket foundations. However, the number of jacket pin piles required (828) is greater than the number of monopiles (207), and installation of jackets is therefore likely to result in active piling over a longer period of time, relative to monopiles. Noise modelling has therefore been undertaken for both monopile and jacket foundations scenarios, with technical detail on piling procedures and schedule provided by the project design teams.

6.3.7 Table 11 details the two pile scenarios modelled.  Two different piling locations have been modelled to provide an understanding of noise propagation at different depths across the site. Further information on the background to noise modelling, including a literature review of the impacts of noise, methodology and analysis is provided in Annex B2, Noise Modelling Technical Report (Subacoustech, 2013).
